stories.headline: Zelensky Says US Too Focused on Middle East, Not Pressing Russia Hard Enough
stories.summary:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told the BBC in an interview at his Kyiv office that delays in US deliveries of anti-ballistic missiles are costing Ukrainian lives. He also said Washington is not pushing Russia hard enough in peace negotiations. "When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor... it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It's not right," he said.

Zelensky called it "strange" that President Donald Trump had posted a picture of himself embracing Vladimir Putin and called him "my friend." Speaking in English, he said: "He's an aggressor, and a killer. He can't be a friend. Just cannot be." He compared the remark to claiming friendship with Adolf Hitler during World War II.

The latest round of talks, mediated in Abu Dhabi earlier this month, made no obvious progress. Zelensky said: "The more we know, the more problems." He said talks are expected to resume in December, and that it is unclear whether European negotiators will be at the table as US envoys announced, with the Kremlin appearing to resist. On Thursday, Trump posted on Truth Social that at his summit with Putin in China last week he had urged Russia to pull back military aggression across Europe, and said a peace deal was "a strong possibility." The US maintains that it is neutral as it seeks a settlement that can hold.

Russian strikes are growing more frequent and deadly, and civilian deaths are at an all-time high. Zelensky said Ukraine can now destroy about 70 percent of Russia's fastest jet-powered drones, while Ukraine launches hundreds of drones at targets in Russia in response.

stories.headline: New Zealand's Ruling Coalition Falls One Seat Short of Majority After Official Count
stories.summary:
New Zealand's governing coalition has fallen one seat short of a parliamentary majority, according to official results released Friday. Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's National Party won 40 of 130 seats, with partners ACT taking 13 and New Zealand First 12. The coalition now needs the centrist Opportunity Party, which won seven seats, to remain in power; if no deal is reached, the country could return to the polls.

Preliminary results on election day, 7 November, had projected a slim lead for the right-leaning bloc. The official tally shows it lost two seats to special votes, those cast by people overseas or outside their home electorates, which typically skew left. Labour won 36 seats, the Greens 17 and Te Pati Maori five. A Labour-led government is not mathematically possible, even with Opportunity's support.

Luxon said negotiations "may be challenging" and will take time, adding: "Kiwis won't thank us for rushing to an agreement that falls apart or for sending them back to the polls." Labour leader Chris Hipkins said his party ran an incredible campaign and that more New Zealanders voted for change than for the status quo, but acknowledged Labour has no negotiating power. Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong said her party will negotiate with National but that all options remain open.

The campaign was shaped by a sluggish economy, high unemployment and rising living costs. National pledged lower taxes, cheaper energy and more defence focus, while Labour campaigned on cutting healthcare, transport and fuel costs and expanding social housing.

stories.headline: Blanche Orders Justice Department Lawyers to Fight Wave of 97,000 ICE Detainee Petitions
stories.summary:
Attorney General Todd Blanche issued a three-page memo Tuesday directing Justice Department civil litigators outside immigration work to help fight a flood of habeas corpus petitions from detained migrants. The petitions ask federal courts to review whether their detention is lawful. Blanche called the filings "frivolous" and an attempt to "thwart President Trump's promise to the American people to prioritize their safety and security."

The department has received 97,000 such petitions since January 2025, including nearly 10,000 since October, compared with a few hundred in a typical year. The surge followed an administration policy change denying bond hearings to migrants arrested inside the United States, including long-term residents. Without access to immigration judges for bond, detainees have gone directly to federal district courts. The memo calls on attorneys from the Antitrust, Civil Rights and Civil divisions, among others, to assist overwhelmed US attorneys' offices.

Blanche also accused judges who have granted petitions of being "corrupt" and of seeking to release criminal aliens into communities. Supporters of the administration say the filings clog courts and obstruct enforcement, noting DHS figures showing nearly 1.2 million removals to date. Immigrant advocates and critics of the policy argue that detainees have a constitutional right to challenge their confinement and that the volume of petitions reflects widespread concern about the legality of the no-bond policy, which courts have repeatedly granted relief against. The Supreme Court is also set to scrutinize a key pillar of the deportation system.

stories.headline: Thirteen Dead, Thirteen Missing After Flooding at Illegal Gold Mine in Indonesia
stories.summary:
Indonesian authorities confirmed Thursday that 13 people have died and their bodies were recovered from a flooded illegal gold mine in Bogor, West Java. At least 13 more are thought to be missing. About 26 miners were digging in an open-pit mine roughly 100 meters deep on Monday night when torrential rain caused a nearby river to overflow and flood two shafts.

Search-and-rescue crews are using ropes to reach the dark, narrow and slippery shafts, which continue to flood from below. Ambulances and medical staff are waiting at the surface. Jakarta Search and Rescue Office head Desiana Kartika Bahari said teams are monitoring water conditions and shaft access, citing depth, narrow passages and limited lighting as key constraints.

Small-scale gold mining is banned in Indonesia but remains widespread, and studies show the illegal industry has surged over the past decade, often alongside rising gold prices that hit record highs in early 2026. The mine sits in an area permitted to state-owned Aneka Tambang, which said the mine was not its own and operated without authorization. West Java police said they uncovered 24 illegal mining cases across the province in October and November alone.

Experts say official figures understate the problem. Former anti-corruption official Laode M Syarif said every illegal mine has "backing," usually from police, military or senior local officials, making the trade hard to eradicate.

stories.headline: Thanksgiving Storm Cancels Hundreds of Flights and Leaves Thousands Without Power
stories.summary:
A severe weather system disrupted Thanksgiving Day across the United States, with hundreds of flights cancelled and thousands of customers without electricity. Coverage from 11 outlets described the scale of the disruption during one of the busiest travel periods of the year.

In California, the National Weather Service warned that coastal water levels could exceed 8 feet (2.4 metres) in some areas on Thursday. If that happens, the levels could break records set along the state's coastline just last month.

The weather follows a nor'easter that earlier forced Macy's to postpone its Thanksgiving parade for the first time. Forecasters and utilities continue to monitor conditions, and further delays and outages remain possible as the holiday travel weekend begins.

stories.headline: North Korea's Kim Inspects Nuclear Material Factories, Vows to Build More Weapons
stories.summary:
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited facilities that produce nuclear materials and called for building more nuclear weapons, according to state media. The visit came days after he ignored an offer from President Donald Trump to meet during Trump's recent trip to Asia.

The Korean Central News Agency said Kim inspected two nuclear materials production factories, one newly opened and one being expanded. Photos showed Kim and military officials among rows of what appeared to be uranium-enrichment centrifuges and halls displaying what were believed to be warheads. Kim also visited a nuclear-powered equipment production base and a nuclear research institute.

Kim said the nuclear arsenal is an "irreversible reality" and called the deployment of low-yield battlefield nuclear weapons "crucial and urgent." He accused the United States of encouraging regional allies to acquire nuclear-powered submarines and share nuclear weapons.

Experts say Kim wants to display his arsenal and reaffirm his rejection of talks on denuclearization. The U.S. position that North Korea must denuclearize remains unchanged, even as Trump has said he is willing to meet Kim.

stories.headline: Democrats Plan to Cut Off Funding for Iran War, but Next Steps Unclear
stories.summary:
Incoming Democratic majorities in Congress have made cutting off funding for the U.S. war with Iran a top priority. President Trump launched the war nine months ago without congressional input, and Democrats say voters demanded action on the issue in this month's elections.

The open question is what happens after funding is cut. Democrats must determine whether they can force the president to end the conflict without jeopardizing U.S. forces in the region.

Republicans and the administration have generally defended the president's authority to conduct military operations and have warned that cutting funds could endanger troops. Democrats counter that Congress holds the power of the purse and was bypassed in the decision to go to war. The debate is likely to shape the new Congress's early agenda.

stories.headline: Mexico's Sheinbaum Rebukes US Over New DEA Anonymous Tip Line
stories.summary:
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum criticized a new anonymous tip line created by the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration to report cartel activity and corrupt officials. She called it "interference" in her country's affairs.

"The DEA has plenty of work to do in its own country. A lot," Sheinbaum said, according to the Associated Press. "The first thing it should do is investigate corruption in the United States."

The dispute adds to tension over U.S. counternarcotics efforts and Mexican sovereignty. U.S. officials have argued the tip line helps combat cartels and official corruption, while Mexico's government says such efforts should be coordinated through established channels.

stories.headline: Two Italians Killed in Drone Strike in Kuwait as Iran Denies Responsibility
stories.summary:
Two Italian technicians working for the German arms manufacturer Rheinmetall were killed in a strike on a facility in Kuwait, according to Italy's foreign ministry. Kuwait and Italy have both blamed Iran for the attack. Iran has denied responsibility, with armed forces spokesperson Abolfazl Shekarchi saying "no military or offensive operations have been conducted" by its military.

Kuwait's defence ministry said earlier that four people had been injured by falling shrapnel after several drones from Iran were detected and intercepted. The injured included the two Italians, a Kuwaiti national and a Pakistani national. Italian media reported that the two men were working at an air defence detection station, performing maintenance on systems used by the Kuwaiti Armed Forces. One was reported to be 36 and the other 65 and nearing retirement. Kuwait's Army described the target as a "vital site in the country" and condemned what it called "heinous Iranian aggression."

The attack comes just over a week after Kuwait said it repelled overnight Iranian drone attacks on an airbase hosting US forces, the first strikes on the country in more than two months. Recent exchanges of fire between the US and Iran, along with deadlocked negotiations, have raised fears of a major escalation. The war began in late February when the US and Israel attacked Iran, which retaliated with missiles and drones aimed at Israel and Gulf Arab states hosting US military assets.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni offered condolences to the families of the victims. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Europe must "step up pressure on Iran to end these unacceptable attacks against its neighbours," adding that Gulf security is "a security issue for us all."

stories.headline: UK and Netherlands Bear Brunt of Surge in Iran-Linked Attacks in Europe, Report Finds
stories.summary:
The United Kingdom and the Netherlands have borne the brunt of a surge in hostile activities orchestrated by Iran this year, according to a new report. The findings raise questions about the effectiveness of European efforts to counter such operations.

Separately, German police arrested two Iraqi men alleged to be members of an Iran-linked terrorist organization. The group is said to have targeted US, Israeli and Jewish institutions in Europe.

The report comes as the conflict between Iran and the US and Israel, which began in late February, continues to spill across the Middle East and beyond. European officials have increasingly warned about Iranian activity on the continent. The findings are likely to add pressure on European governments to strengthen counterintelligence and security measures.

stories.headline: FIFA Says Cyberattack Stole 'Limited Set of Personal and Business Information'
stories.summary:
FIFA, soccer's international governing body, said Thursday that it was the victim of a criminal cyberattack resulting in unauthorized access to a "limited set of personal and business information." The organization did not immediately detail what data was taken or how many people were affected.

The disclosure comes amid separate scrutiny of the organization in Washington. Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee sent letters on Wednesday to a number of current and former FIFA employees, including some who held senior positions, asking them to attend interviews as part of a congressional investigation into the so-called Fifa Forward Enterprise scandal.

FIFA president Gianni Infantino could be subpoenaed to give evidence in January, according to reports. It is not known whether the cyberattack is connected to the congressional inquiry.

stories.headline: Carney's Major Projects Bill C-39 Draws Opposition from Conservative Leader Poilievre
stories.summary:
Canadian Conservative Party Leader Pierre Poilievre pledged to vote against Prime Minister Mark Carney's latest effort to speed up federal reviews of major projects. He accused the government of centralizing too much power and steamrolling over workers' rights.

The bill, C-39, is part of Carney's push to accelerate approvals for large infrastructure and energy projects. Supporters of such measures argue that faster reviews are needed to attract investment and build economic capacity, while critics say they concentrate authority in the federal government and weaken protections.

A similar debate is under way in the United States, where the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 passed the Senate 62-33 and is now being debated in the House. The permitting reform bill is backed by industry, while advocates warn it would gut key clean water protections without meaningfully speeding major energy projects.

stories.headline: Trump Demands Investigation Into GDP Data Revisions, Alleging Without Evidence That Figures Were Understated Before Midterms
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump on Thursday called for an investigation into the government's economic statistics. In a Thanksgiving Day post on Truth Social, he alleged without providing evidence that initial gross domestic product figures released before the midterm elections were deliberately understated. The call came after the Commerce Department revised its estimate of third-quarter growth upward. Trump accused his own administration's Commerce Department of a "purposeful" move to under-report growth.

Revisions to GDP are routine and reflect more complete information that becomes available after the initial estimates are published. Axios noted that the allegations could renew concerns about political interference in the production of the economic data that underpin trillions of dollars in decisions by businesses, investors and policymakers. Several outlets described the president as seizing on a routine data revision to support an allegation of election interference.

The president has argued that his economic policies are working and has pushed back on coverage he sees as ignoring administration wins. On Thursday he also attacked New York Times reporter David Sanger as a "lowlife" after the paper published an analysis of his varying success in moving markets. Supporters of the president have long argued that official statistics and media coverage understate economic gains, while critics and many economists say the request threatens the independence of the statistical agencies.

It was not immediately clear what form an investigation would take or which agency would carry it out. The comments come after a poor midterm result for Republicans and as the administration continues to press its trade agenda.

stories.headline: Update: China, Japan and Other Trading Partners Protest Proposed US Tariff Hikes
stories.summary:
China, Japan and other US trading partners have voiced anger and regret over the tariff proposals announced by the Trump administration. The new development is the international reaction, following the US Trade Representative's announcement of proposed duties on China, the European Union and a dozen other jurisdictions.

Under the proposals, China faces the highest rate, up to 40 percent, followed by Vietnam at up to 35 percent, with others facing 20 or 25 percent. The affected economies include the EU, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, India, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand and Bangladesh. Some rates would be effectively reduced by caps in deals the countries previously struck with Washington.

USTR Jamieson Greer said the measures would "level the playing field for American workers," arguing that partners have for decades pursued industrial strategies that suppress wages and distort markets. The duties are not expected to take effect until next year and must go through public consultation and potentially hearings. They rest on the USTR's authority to address foreign trade practices, after the Supreme Court ruled the earlier Liberation Day tariffs illegal.

Economists warn that tariffs can raise consumer prices and dampen global trade, while the administration says they will boost manufacturing and narrow the trade deficit. The levies are likely to face legal challenges.

stories.headline: Update: Egyptian Authorities Arrest Motorist Over Cairo Tanker Crash That Killed 31
stories.summary:
Egyptian authorities have arrested a man accused of causing the tanker crash and fire on Cairo's Ring Road that killed 31 people. The public prosecutor's office said the motorist confessed to driving at 110 km/h and clipping the tanker with the side of his car while changing lanes. The death toll has risen from the at least 30 reported earlier.

According to the prosecutor, the collision made him lose control, and one of the tanker's tyres burst, sending it into the central reservation, where it overturned and spilled fuel that ignited. State media had earlier cited sources saying a fallen high-voltage cable caused the tanker driver to lose control. The suspect, who has not been named, was travelling with his father. Twenty-one others were injured in the Warraq neighbourhood and treated for burns and smoke inhalation.

The raised motorway was reopened hours after the crash. A cabinet minister said 10 million Egyptian pounds had been donated to victims' families, and the sports minister said state-run celebratory activities would be cancelled. Egypt has suffered several deadly fires in recent years, and road collisions, attributed to poor maintenance and traffic violations, kill thousands annually.

stories.headline: Update: Zelenskyy Says Russia Preparing Major Attack on Ukrainian Energy Infrastructure
stories.summary:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Thursday that Russia is preparing another major attack on Ukraine's energy infrastructure, logistics and critical services. His warning came as US envoy Jared Kushner said Russian President Vladimir Putin has "shown restraint" in the war by agreeing not to use nuclear weapons.

Separately, a senior adviser to Zelenskyy said Ukraine has for the first time used a laser weapon to shoot down a Russian jet-powered drone. The development points to Kyiv's efforts to field new air-defense technologies as Russian strikes continue to target the power grid.

The statements come amid heightened tension over the war's trajectory, with recent Russian nuclear rhetoric and European concern over what Washington, Moscow and Beijing may be discussing. Kushner's characterization of Putin's conduct is likely to draw differing reactions: supporters of the administration's diplomacy see it as evidence of progress, while critics argue it understates Russia's continued attacks on civilian infrastructure.

stories.headline: Bipartisan Push to Regulate Artificial Intelligence Faces Obstacles in Congress
stories.summary:
Key Republicans and Democrats in Congress are pressing for quick action to address the risks of artificial intelligence after years of legislative paralysis. According to The New York Times, the push is driven by voter concerns and by industry warnings about the economic and even existential perils of unchecked AI development. The effort comes as markets have been rattled by a sell-off in AI-linked technology stocks and by scrutiny of the White House's role in reinstating Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang.

Obstacles remain substantial. Lawmakers are divided over whether federal rules should preempt state laws, how much to restrain an industry seen as central to U.S. economic competitiveness, and how to balance safety measures against competition with China. Industry lobbying and the crowded post-election legislative calendar, which includes a stopgap spending bill, also complicate any quick action.

The issue has taken on political weight after this month's midterm elections. A Guardian opinion column argued that Democrats lack a compelling AI plan and must make the technology work for the public rather than for what it called tech oligarchs. Many Republicans, for their part, stress the need to avoid heavy-handed rules that could hand an advantage to foreign rivals, while also voicing concern over safety and the power of large technology firms. Whether the shared urgency produces a bill in the coming session remains uncertain.

stories.headline: Mandelson Refused to Sell Global Counsel Stake Despite Conflict Concerns, Files Reveal
stories.summary:
Peter Mandelson, Britain's disgraced former ambassador to the United States, refused to sell his stake in the lobbying firm Global Counsel despite government concerns about conflicts of interest, according to official documents published Thursday. The files indicate he declined because he wanted more money for the holding.

The documents add detail to the controversy surrounding his tenure as ambassador, during which officials raised questions about whether his business interests could clash with his diplomatic role. Global Counsel is a lobbying and advisory firm that Mandelson helped found, and it counts corporate clients with interests in Washington and London.

The release is likely to sharpen scrutiny of how his appointment was vetted and how the government handled the concerns it identified. It was covered by outlets across the spectrum, including Bloomberg, the New York Post and The Guardian. Further political fallout in Britain is expected as lawmakers and opposition parties review the files.

stories.headline: Gérard Depardieu to Stand Trial for Alleged 2018 Rape of Actress Charlotte Arnould
stories.summary:
A Paris appeals court on Thursday confirmed that French film actor Gérard Depardieu must stand trial for the alleged rape of actress Charlotte Arnould in 2018. Arnould, who was 22 at the time, reported the alleged assault several days after going to his Paris home to rehearse a play. She has waived her right to anonymity, and her lawyer called the ruling a historic first.

Depardieu, 77, had contested his indictment on two counts of rape. The court ruled he would be tried over the events of 7 August 2018 but not over a second alleged rape at a hotel six days later. His lawyer said the court had partly ruled in his favor and that the defense would look into an appeal to the Court of Cassation. In a 2023 letter in Le Figaro, Depardieu denied the allegations, saying there was never any coercion or violence.

The ruling follows his conviction last year for sexually assaulting two women on a film set, which brought an 18-month suspended sentence and placement on the sex offenders register. He dropped his appeal last week and apologized for his behavior on that set. He is also under a separate investigation, alongside author Michel Houellebecq, over alleged sexual offenses on the 2018 film Thalasso.

stories.headline: Cheaper Generic HIV Prevention Injection Reaches Africa
stories.summary:
The first global shipment of a generic version of lenacapavir, a twice-yearly injection to prevent HIV, arrived in Zambia on Wednesday, the Global Fund said. Uganda is expected to receive supplies in the coming days, and Zimbabwe early next year, with other countries to follow.

The drug is nearly 100 percent effective at preventing infection and is expected to cost about $40 per person annually. The original version, developed by Gilead Sciences, cost about $28,000 a year in the United States and became available in sub-Saharan Africa only a year ago. A 2024 trial of more than 5,000 adolescent girls and young women in Uganda and South Africa found no infections among those who received it.

More than 189,000 people in 10 countries have received a first injection, and the Global Fund expects 24 countries to have supplies by year's end. Working with the U.S. government, it aims to reach at least three million people by the end of 2028, eventually covering 120 low- and middle-income countries. Sub-Saharan Africa accounts for nearly two-thirds of people living with HIV, among about 41 million worldwide.

stories.headline: Update: US Formally Announces Proposed Tariffs on China, EU and a Dozen Other Jurisdictions
stories.summary:
The US Trade Representative on Wednesday formally announced a new round of proposed tariffs on imports from China, the European Union and 12 other jurisdictions, including Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, India, Vietnam and Switzerland. China faces the highest proposed rate, up to 40%, followed by Vietnam at up to 35%, with the others facing 20% or 25%. The USTR published detailed reports on how each jurisdiction's trade practices allegedly affect American commerce.

The duties are not expected to take effect until next year and must go through public consultation and potentially hearings. Some rates would be effectively reduced by caps on tariffs that Trump previously agreed with individual countries. The White House began investigating foreign trade practices in March after the Supreme Court ruled that Trump's earlier Liberation Day tariffs, imposed under emergency powers, were illegal. The new approach relies on the USTR's authority to address unfair foreign trade practices, which some analysts say rests on a stronger legal foundation.

USTR Jamieson Greer said the measures would "level the playing field for American workers and chart a new, more sustainable course for the world economy," accusing trading partners of industrial strategies built on wage and labor suppression and other market-distorting practices. Economists warn that tariffs can fuel inflation and raise consumer prices if businesses pass on higher costs, while also dampening global trade. Trump has pressed ahead with the policy despite poor Republican results in the midterm elections, arguing it will boost manufacturing, create jobs and cut the trade deficit. The levies are likely to face legal challenges.

stories.headline: FCC Approves SpaceX Plan to Launch One Million Data-Center Satellites
stories.summary:
The Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday approved SpaceX's plan to launch up to one million satellites to build data centers in orbit, the first approval of its kind. The project, called Starmind, would use solar power to process data for artificial intelligence and relay results to Earth. The satellites would operate in low-Earth orbit at 500 to 2,000 km and communicate through the existing Starlink network of more than 10,000 satellites.

Under the license, deployment must begin by November 2033, with 10% of satellites in orbit by November 2035 and 50% by November 2038. SpaceX has said it hopes to launch its first Starmind satellite next year. It is unclear whether the full million will be launched or whether SpaceX sought a higher number than it plans to use.

FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said the project "opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America's leadership and growth." Elon Musk called it "a great asset to America and the world." Amazon criticized the plan as a "lofty ambition rather than a real plan," and US astronomers said it would significantly undermine the public's ability to observe the night sky. Some experts see space-based computing as a response to growing opposition to terrestrial data centers, which analysts say was a factor in Republican losses in the midterms. Satellite engineer Sir Martin Sweeting called the idea technically feasible but questioned whether it makes sense at scale.

stories.headline: Oil Tanker Sinks Off Ibiza, Killing One Crew Member
stories.summary:
The Malta-flagged chemical tanker Med Emre sank about 25 nautical miles off Ibiza, carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel. All 17 crew were rescued, but seven were taken to hospitals in Valencia and Ibiza, and one later died. The others reportedly suffered minor injuries such as hypothermia.

Rescuers in Valencia received a distress call around 22:30 local time Wednesday, and minutes later the vessel reported a leak and said it was listing at 90 degrees. The ship had been traveling from Algeciras to Barcelona. The cause of the sinking is unclear.

Authorities are assessing possible environmental damage using an aircraft and Spain's pollution control vessel Clara Campoamor. Balearic Islands President Marga Prohens said there was little information yet about a possible spill. The area's marine environment has been on the Unesco World Heritage List since 1999 and includes dense Posidonia oceanica seagrass meadows. Spain suffered one of its worst environmental disasters in 2002, when the Prestige tanker spilled more than 60,000 tonnes of fuel oil off Galicia.

stories.headline: Seven Injured, Four Critically, in Bangkok Oil Refinery Explosion
stories.summary:
An explosion and fire at the Phra Khanong oil refinery in eastern Bangkok injured seven people, four of them critically, local officials said. The facility is run by Bangchak Corporation, and the blast occurred around 14:45 local time. Black smoke was visible across the city's skyline.

The company said the fire was brought under control and extinguished within 30 minutes, and that the cause is under investigation. Bangkok authorities sent a mobile alert urging residents to avoid the area, and officials told people nearby to leave. The Erawan Emergency Medical Centre said it was treating four "red" cases and three less severe "yellow" cases.

Bangchak shut down production at the site, which can process up to 120,000 barrels a day. The company has a second refinery in Chonburi province with capacity of about 180,000 barrels daily. A previous explosion at the Bangkok refinery in July 2012 caused a fire but no reported injuries.
